tagline: River Road links former canal towns along the James River corridor.
intro: River Road leaves Scottsville beside the James and the railway, then climbs out of the valley. Farther east, Route 6 alternately approaches the river and veers away from it. Its Virginia Byway designation extends to SR 650 near Manakin. The state’s designation identifies scenic roads offering alternative destinations for travelers.

This corridor carried canal traffic before railway tracks occupied the towpath. The James River and Kanawha Canal sought a connection with the Ohio River, but war interrupted construction and railways became competitors. In 1880, the canal passed to a new railway company, which began laying tracks along it. The Richmond and Allegheny Railroad used that route, and the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway leased it in 1888 before purchasing it.

From Scottsville, head through Kidds Store to Fork Union, then cross the Rivanna before Columbia. The road briefly follows the James valley into Goochland County and returns toward the river at Goochland. At Goochland, Route 6 shares US 522 past the county offices before US 522 turns across the James. Continue through Manakin and Sabot, where the highway widens to four divided lanes. At Richmond Country Club, River Road branches south; Route 6 continues toward Henrico as Patterson Avenue.

moments.title: Scottsville
moments.text: Scottsville occupies a horseshoe bend in the James, where a canal port once handled traffic bound for Richmond. A wagon road connected it with Staunton and brought Shenandoah Valley agricultural produce into town. The James River and Kanawha Canal made Scottsville its largest port town, but the intended connection to the Ohio River was never completed. Union soldiers damaged the canal works, disrupting trade. Railway tracks subsequently occupied the old towpath. Route 6 now runs beside the river and railway through town before climbing away from the valley. In 1985, the Army Corps of Engineers built a levee around the town’s lowest section after repeated flooding.

moments.title: Columbia
moments.text: The James and Rivanna meet at Columbia, formerly called Point of Fork. That junction linked Richmond and Lynchburg by the James and Charlottesville by the Rivanna. Columbia developed a bateau freight line for the tobacco trade and later became a stagecoach stop between Richmond and Staunton. Passenger rail service ended in 1958; floods from Hurricanes Camille and Agnes destroyed homes and businesses in 1969 and 1972. After a resident referendum, Columbia ceased to be an incorporated town in 2016. The Rivanna Connexion canal once joined the James River and Kanawha Canal here; sediment now mostly buries the connecting locks outside town.

moments.title: Goochland
moments.text: Goochland’s other name, Goochland Court House, identifies its role as the county seat just north of the James. Dabney Cosby built the courthouse in 1826 as a two-story brick building with a temple form and a projecting Tuscan portico. The square also contains a stone jail dating to 1848 and the original brick clerk’s office. Route 6 shares US 522 through the center of the community before the two routes separate near the river. A monument to Goochland County’s Confederate dead was added to the square in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century.
